title: Tool Handshake & Structured Delivery — PRD (wip)
content:
Status: WIP. This doc is a working PRD for a succinct, lower-friction tool-handshake and structured-delivery surface on the Hosted API. Focus: (1) make tool calling predictable over streaming responses, (2) let SDKs materialize typed outputs and stable retry/ordering semantics, (3) provide fallbacks for text-only clients and degraded-network conditions.

Background/context:
- We've deployed streaming generation and basic tool-calling primitives in the hosted API. Customers want: deterministic tool invocation semantics when using streaming (so that a downstream service can react mid-response), typed structured output support (JSON-first responses with schema hints), and SDK ergonomics that make wiring callbacks and handlers straightforward across languages.
- Current pain points observed in early customers and SDK experiments: broken ordering when reconnecting during a streaming tool call, ambiguity over which sequence of partial tokens constitutes a tool invocation, and ad-hoc parsing strategies across SDKs that leak complexity to integrators.

Goals (what success looks like):
- Behavioral: tool invocations over streaming have exactly-once semantics from the customer's perspective for the canonical happy-path (network partitions and retries handled via idempotency tokens).
- Developer ergonomics: SDK wiring for tool handlers is < 10 lines for common cases (register handler, call API, receive typed result).
- Operational: streaming tool call error rate <= 0.5% (for production customers after rollout), end-to-end 95th pct call latency within 1.2x of non-tool streaming baseline for small payloads.
- Adoption: 30% of new hosted-api streaming customers use structured-delivery primitives within 3 months of GA.

Non-goals:
- This PRD does not specify private-dedicated deployment networking (that will be a follow-on).
- Does not introduce new model-level training; assumes existing model variants provide tool-call tokens or structured hints.

High-level design overview:
1) Explicit stream event envelope
- All server-streamed frames use a compact envelope: {event_type, event_id, seq, payload}. Payload types include: text_chunk, tool_call_start, tool_call_arg, tool_call_end, structured_output, error, checkpoint.
- event_id is a short UUID per logical event (eg. per model response). seq is monotonically increasing per event_id to allow recomposition after reconnects.
- This allows SDKs to rehydrate partial streams, detect missing seq ranges, and request replay/resume.

2) Tool-handshake lifecycle
- tool_call_start contains tool_descriptor (name, version, canonical args spec reference) and an idempotency_token.
- tool_call_arg frames stream arguments (for large blobs) flagged with arg_name and chunk_idx.
- tool_call_end marks logical end and includes an expected callback contract (callback_url or sdk_handler_hint).
- Server may emit tool_call_result frames when model returns a tool-result or structured_output when the model finishes.
- Server guarantees: if tool_call_start and tool_call_end are received for an event_id and seq series, subscribers will see either a tool_call_result or an explicit error frame.

3) Structured-delivery primitives
- Models may emit structured_output frames with content that is JSON or typed-binary (base64). Each structured_output includes a schema_hint: a compact schema id and optional minimal schema snapshot.
- SDKs will offer automatic schema validation and typed deserialization helpers (e.g., map to typed objects, validation errors surfaced as SDK exceptions).

4) SDK ergonomics (patterns and examples)
- Core primitives for SDKs: register_tool_handler(name, handler_fn), stream_response(request, on_event), resume_stream(token, on_event).
- Example (pseudocode):

  handler = lambda ctx, args: call_customer_service(args)
  sdk.register_tool_handler("search_db", handler)

  def on_event(e):
    if e.type == "structured_output":
      obj = sdk.deserialize(e.payload)  # validated against schema_hint
      app.handle(obj)
    elif e.type == "tool_call":
      # SDK will route to registered handler and emit the result back to the server in-band
      result = sdk.invoke_local_handler(e.tool_descriptor, e.args, idempotency=e.idempotency_token)
      sdk.emit_tool_result(e.event_id, result)

- Backpressure & flow control: SDK exposes a simple credit-based API for consumers that process tool results. The client can supply max_concurrent_tool_handlers and per-handler timeouts. The runtime will buffer up to N bytes per connection and begin applying shedding strategies if clients fall behind (emit checkpoint frames that allow server to drop partial data safely with a resumable token).

5) Reconnect & resume semantics
- Clients receive a resume_token every 30s or on explicit checkpoint frames. When reconnecting, client sends last_seen_event_id + seq. Server will replay frames from that position or emit a tombstone if that history expired.
- If a tool_call was started but no tool_call_end was received before disconnect, server will mark it as "incomplete" and return the same tool_call_start when resuming. SDKs must use idempotency_token to avoid double-invocation.

Edge cases and fallbacks:
- Text-only clients: if the client can't consume event envelopes, the server will fall back to a best-effort linearized text stream (merging structured frames into human-readable text). Documented degradation: loss of schema metadata, inability to perform reliable resume for tool calls.
- Tool-side timeouts: a tool handler can optionally return an intermediate partial result + continuation hint; server will surface both partial and final frames.

Telemetry & observability requirements:
- Per-event tracing id (traceable to request id, event_id) emitted to Console for: tool_call_start, tool_call_end, tool_call_result, structured_output, resume, checkpoint, stream_error.
- Metrics: tool-call-success-rate, tool-handler-latency-p99, stream-reconnect-rate, resume-success-rate, structured-validate-fail-rate.
- Cost visibility: per-tool token count and per-structured-output bytes emitted.

Security & compatibility notes:
- tool_descriptor references must be whitelisted per account for hosted customers (avoid arbitrary callbacks).
- Idempotency token must be cryptographically random client-generated string. Server will store token->result mapping for duration T (configurable per plan) to enforce exactly-once semantics in the happy path.

Open questions (needs product/engineering decisions):
- Duration T for idempotency retention by default (1 hour vs 24 hours). Tradeoff: larger T increases storage and reduces accidental double-invoke.
- Should the envelope use numeric seqs or vector clocks for multi-shard responses? Numeric seqs are simpler but require careful shard coordination.
- Level of schema snapshot included in structured_output: embed minimal inline snapshot vs pointer to schema registry. Cost vs convenience tradeoff.

Implementation phases (proposal):
- Phase 0 (experiment): server emits event envelope for structured_output only. SDKs parse envelope but do not provide automated handler wiring. (Q1 2025, internal beta)
- Phase 1 (canary): add tool_call_start/tool_call_end frames + idempotency token; SDKs in Python + Node provide register_tool_handler and basic resume semantics. Console shows per-tool metrics. (Q2 2025, invited customers)
- Phase 2 (GA): full SDK family (Go, Java, Ruby) support, schema registry integration, and UI for schema hints in Console. Backward compat shim for text-only clients and migration docs. (Q4 2025)

Rollout & migration notes for customers:
- Migration stance: Gradual opt-in. Existing clients keep exact same non-enveloped streaming behavior unless they set "envelope=true" in request headers. This gives us ability to iterate on envelope semantics without breaking.
- Migration checklist for customers: update SDK, register handlers if using local handlers, verify schema compatibility with provided schema_hint.

Risks and mitigations:
- Risk: Increased complexity in SDKs leads to client-side bugs. Mitigation: provide thorough end-to-end integration tests and a test harness that simulates partial reconnects.
- Risk: Storage overhead for idempotency mappings. Mitigation: tiered retention; use LRU eviction for small plans.

Open action items (owner):
- Confirm idempotency retention default (Elena) -> decision needed 2024-10-01.
- Prototype envelope replay with resume_token in serving-runtime (Ravi).
- Draft Python SDK surface and example app (Sofie).
- Telemetry spec (Jonah) - list of metrics + traces to wire to Console.

Appendix: short examples
1) Minimal event envelope (text representation):
  {event_type: "tool_call_start", event_id: "evt_abc123", seq: 1, payload: {tool: "search_db", idempotency: "tok_xxx", descriptor_ref: "tools::search-db:v1"}}
  {event_type: "tool_call_arg", event_id: "evt_abc123", seq: 2, payload: {arg_name: "query", chunk_idx: 0, chunk: "how many users signed up..."}}
  {event_type: "tool_call_end", event_id: "evt_abc123", seq: 3, payload: {}}
  {event_type: "tool_call_result", event_id: "evt_abc123", seq: 4, payload: {result_id: "res_01", body: {count: 123, top_sources: ["s1","s2"]}}}

2) SDK pseudocode for resume:
  token = client.start_stream(req, on_event)
  # on reconnect
  client.resume_stream(last_seen_event_id, last_seq, on_event)
Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally pragmatic: small envelope with clear sequencing makes it easier to implement resume and idempotency. Please challenge the choice of field names and retention semantics.
- Want to lock major API/SDK invariants by end of Q4 2024 so engineering can prototype Q1 components.

----
Notes-to-self: copy examples into spec repo, add a sample server implementation that emits envelope frames over HTTP/2 and WebSocket. Also add an integration test that simulates network partition and verifies idempotency with duplicate resume attempts.
